Dépasser les idées reçues : la chercheus: Moving Past Preconceptions: Researcher Liza Hammar Reframes the Debate on the Veil
Liza Hammar critique le débat sur le hij: Liza Hammar critiques the debate on the hijab, deconstructs the idea of “choice” and exposes the effects of laws like Bill 21.
Conférence avec Liza Hammar au Bâtiment: Lecture with Liza Hammar at Bâtiment 7, in the Grand atelier. Photo by JC.
<strong>Au Québec, comme en France, le v: In Quebec, as in France, the Muslim veil is criticized in the name of secularism, the protection of women, Western values or gender equality. In response, lines of defence are forming around individual freedom, against the erasure of the women who wear it and their exclusion from certain jobs, notably because of Bills 21 and 94.
<strong>Avec <em>Le hijab, leur obsessio: With Le hijab, leur obsession et nous (The Hijab, Their Obsession and Us), researcher Liza Hammar tries to break the vicious circle. At the invitation of her Quebec publisher, La rue Dorion, the author met her audience on April 9 at Bâtiment 7, where she offered a critical reading of “fixed” conceptions of the question of choosing to wear the hijab, of the fantasy of “unveiling,” and of analyses that leave out issues of race, gender, class and religion.
<strong>Dans <em>Lettre à mon hijab</em>: In Lettre à mon hijab (Letter to My Hijab), the final chapter of the book, she sums up her personal position this way: “You are not the option most favourable to my material comfort, binding myself to you is even unreasonable given Islamophobia around the world, but life cannot always be guided by the quest for safety. Life is above all made of God, of the pursuit of justice, of resistance – and giving up has never freed anyone.”
Dans le Grand atelier du<l1> Bâtiment 7<: In the Grand atelier at<l1> Bâtiment 7</l1>, about forty people take their seats on chairs packed tightly in rows. The venue, marked by years of community struggles and self-managed initiatives, immediately lends the gathering a political tone. The evening takes the form of a dense, almost head-on dialogue between author Liza Hammar and political scientist Fella Hadj Kaddour, before an attentive audience familiar with the debates that run through Quebec.
Liza Hammar parle avec une retenue qui c: Liza Hammar speaks with a restraint that commands attention. Nothing in her posture is left to chance, but as the conversation goes on, the researcher's rigour gives way to a more heartfelt, almost intimate voice. This tension between rigour and sensitivity is no accident: her favourite book is The Little Prince by Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, a text she says she has never put down since adolescence, and whose way of linking apparent simplicity with depth can be felt here.
Née dans un village kabyle d’Algérie, el: Born in a Kabyle village in Algeria, she emigrated to France at the age of seven, where she grew up, studied and became involved in various activist spaces. Today a doctoral student in literary studies at UQAM, she is researching the notion of reparation in feminist, decolonial and auto-theoretical fields. Her path spans several registers (academic, political and literary) that she refuses to separate. Her book extends this approach, which holds theoretical analysis and lived experience together.
D’emblée, Liza Hammar remet en question: Right from the start, Liza Hammar questions the relevance of the hijab debate, which she calls an “intellectual dead end” when it is reduced to a question of individual choice. For decades, she explains, Muslim women have been summoned to prove their capacity to choose. But, she says flatly, “I don't want to prove to my tormentors that I'm free, I'm turning my back on their cynicism.”
L’exigence, qui oblige les femmes en hij: This demand, which forces women who wear the hijab to justify themselves constantly, confines more than it liberates, in her view, especially since “no one is really worried about whether we're actually free or not – because otherwise, we aren't free for other reasons, but strangely, no one cares about that.”
Ce déplacement est central : au lieu d’i: This shift is central: instead of examining the social, political and economic conditions in which this choice is made, the debate focuses on individual validation and masks, she says, the concrete effects of the laws. “These are extremely violent laws,” she says in an interview, referring to Quebec measures such as Bill 21 and Bill 94. “They don't have the same histories as those in France,” she specifies, “but they have the same effects and target the same women.”
L’automne dernier, le gouvernement de la: Last fall, the Coalition avenir Québec government adopted Bill 94, which aims to tighten the rules of Bill 21 to ensure the religious neutrality of the state in public space. Faced with widespread criticism, the premier at the time, François Legault, responded by writing on social media on November 27, 2025: “Why? Because in Quebec, equality between women and men, and freedom of conscience and religion, are non-negotiable. Because secularism is part of who we are. It is a principle that brings us together, true to our values. Because, yes, that's how we live in Quebec.”
La Cour suprême du Canada a examiné en m: The Supreme Court of Canada heard arguments in March on the validity of the use of the notwithstanding clause in the passage of Bill 21 in Quebec.
<strong>Dévoilement : un récit dominant: Unveiling: a dominant narrative to be deconstructed
Un autre aspect central de l’échange s’a: Another central aspect of the discussion takes aim at the media's glorification of “unveiling” as a universal symbol of liberation. Stories of women who remove their hijab are everywhere in the media and are often presented, according to the guest, as experiences of emancipation.
Au cours de l’entretien, elle précise :: During the interview, she clarifies: “What interests me is not judging these women, but understanding how their stories are used.” In her view, “unveiling in the name of freedom corresponds exactly to the white patriarchal fantasy.” She points to a form of instrumentalization: “We celebrate these stories, but at the same time, we use them without really acknowledging the violence they recount.”
Liza Hammar déconstruit cette narration,: Liza Hammar deconstructs this narrative, detecting in it a normative storytelling, “almost a literary genre in its own right” that does not correspond to real experiences or the multiplicity of situations: forced unveiling in legal contexts, occasional unveiling in intimate spaces, everyday gestures that are not politicized... These situations are deliberately erased in the dominant discourse, she says, because they would make it impossible to maintain a simple opposition between oppression and freedom.
Liza Hammar confie avoir été contrainte,: Liza Hammar confides that as a teenager in France she was forced to remove her hijab to attend lycée, under the enforcement of<l1> the 2004 law</l1>. “I unveiled myself every day for three years in front of my school. It wasn't liberation, it was humiliation,” the guest says. Unveiling in this case, she concludes, is nothing like liberation and becomes a constraint on the body, under the control of an institution that imposes the norm and checks that it is followed.

<strong>Le hijab pour échapper aux norme: The hijab as a way to escape norms?
L’ adolescence a été un moment de bascul: Adolescence was a turning point for Liza Hammar, who says she wore the hijab at that time in her life, but not under compulsion. “At 14, I wanted to remove myself from the male gaze,” she says.
Elle décrit un environnement marqué par: She describes an environment marked by early sexualization and pressure to conform to heterosexual norms. In this context, and contrary to preconceived notions, this gesture expressed not submission to social norms, in her view, but rather an attempt to escape them. “I wanted to be met beyond my body.”
Partant de sa propre expérience, Liza Ha: Drawing on her own experience, Liza Hammar calls for rejecting simplifications and questioning the complexity of people's paths. Families of origin, like hers, can hold a range of positions: religious, secular, atheist. She also stresses that so-called “origin” societies are themselves heterogeneous, and that “the West does not have a monopoly on rejecting the veil.”
<strong>Critique des angles morts des mi: A critique of the blind spots in progressive circles
Fella Hadj Kaddour interroge ensuite l’i: Fella Hadj Kaddour then asks the guest about the criticism she directs in her book at contradictions that, in her view, run through the left and certain feminisms, particularly in France. Liza Hammar describes progressive circles that are able to recognize Islamophobia as a form of racism, but unable to fully embrace the spiritual dimension of the people affected.
Dans ces espaces, dit-elle, être croyant: In these spaces, she says, being a believer exposes you to a form of intellectual disqualification. Indeed, “I was treated as an idiot because I adore God,” she says with a touch of humour. On the ground, she faults part of the left for not fully grasping the consequences of the laws for Muslim women. This is the case in France, but also in Quebec, where, she says in the interview, unions advise women in hijab who are affected by Bills 21 and 94 to wait to be fired rather than resign. “We are facing employment discrimination. The fact that it's legal changes nothing.”
Liza Hammar nuance cependant son propos: Liza Hammar nonetheless qualifies her remarks, admitting that the field is not so empty and that “there are people and collectives doing this work.” She judges, however, that it is not enough: “I think the efforts of these organizations and these activists are not supported openly enough by the rest of the left.”
Au chapitre consacré aux solutions, elle: In the chapter devoted to solutions, she writes: “Faced with extremely violent exclusion from far too many spaces and a terrible precarity affecting Muslim women who wear the hijab, the emergence of Muslim feminisms responds to political isolation.” These are feminisms that, in her view, point to a spectrum of feminist struggles taken up by women “who not only see no opposition between their Islamic identity and their feminism, but move forward with these two belongings concurrently and in a politically enriching way. Approaching Islam from feminist perspectives.”
<strong>Une maison d’édition comme espac: A publishing house as a space of coherence
Le choix de publier aux Éditions de la r: The decision to publish with Éditions de la rue Dorion follows this logic. Founded in Montréal in 2012, this independent house holds a singular place in Quebec's publishing landscape. Its catalogue includes political essays, decolonial thought, critical works, writings emerging from social struggles and translations such as the edifying The Ethnic Cleansing of Palestine by Ilan Pappé. Publishing Le hijab, leur obsession et nous in this setting reflects a political coherence, but is also an editorial risk.
Liza Hammar explique avoir refusé plusie: Liza Hammar explains that she turned down several offers in France so as not to sacrifice the integrity of her argument for a publishing proposal that “wanted to reduce my book to the question of discrimination.” Here, the collaboration with La rue Dorion was built differently because, she says, “they let me take my ideas all the way.”
Elle souligne aussi l’importance des esp: She also stresses the importance of independent publishing spaces: “Taking part in these spaces is also a way of getting other ideas into circulation.”
<strong>Le public interroge : entre la F: Audience questions: between France and Quebec, differences… and similarities
Une fois la parole donnée au public, plu: Once the floor was opened to the audience, several interventions shifted the discussion to a direct comparison between France and Quebec. One question kept coming back: what does it mean to publish such a book in two contexts that are both distinct and increasingly similar?
Liza Hammar répond d’abord par un consta: Liza Hammar first responds with a nuanced observation. “I have the impression that there are fewer and fewer differences, unfortunately, between France and Quebec,” she says, while refusing to conflate the two. She describes her experience in France, where forms of Islamophobia remain, in her view, more head-on, in contrast to Quebec, where racism, she says, sometimes seems harder to grasp: “At first, I had trouble reading it… I didn't understand why it made me uncomfortable.”
Au fil des échanges, une idée s’impose :: As the exchanges go on, one idea takes hold: Islamophobia is not limited to national contexts. “It circulates internationally,” the author insists, pointing to broader dynamics where political discourse, colonial legacies and the rise of certain ideologies intersect.
The evening ends without a clean break. Discussions continue around the author, who signs copies of her book and talks with the audience about certain nuances. There is less certainty here, and more complexity. The debate does not close; it unfolds.
